input: The rate constant $k$ (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures, namely at 300 K and at 340 K, in order to establish how the constant responds when the temperature at which the reaction is carried out is changed. At 300 K, $k$ = 0.077 s-1. At 340 K, $k$ = 2.091 s-1, and it should be made clear that this second value was computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 70 kJ mol-1, so that it is presented as a derived value. Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of $k$ was 4%, which gives an indication of the consistency that was obtained across the repeated measurements at each of the temperatures studied. It is also important to highlight that above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, and because of this difficulty no rate constant is reported above 340 K. The consequence of this limitation is that the results which are available relate only to the temperatures that could actually be studied, and anyone wishing to use these figures should be aware that the behaviour of the reaction at temperatures beyond the studied interval has not been characterised here and cannot be inferred from the reported pair of values without stepping outside the evidence that the measurements provide. The triplicate measurements, for their part, serve to show that the values obtained at each temperature were not isolated readings but were reproduced across repeated measurements under the same conditions.
target: The rate constant $k$ (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at 300 K and at 340 K. At 300 K, $k$ = 0.077 s-1. At 340 K, $k$ = 2.091 s-1; the value at the higher temperature is a derived value, computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 70 kJ mol-1 and presented as a derived value. Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of $k$ was 4%. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K. The pair of values therefore rests on different footing at its two ends. The lower value is a direct measurement, repeated in triplicate, with the stated relative standard deviation. The upper value carries that measurement forward through the Arrhenius relation at the stated activation energy, and its standing depends on the relation and on the activation energy as much as on the measurement itself. The evaporation limit is a limit on sampling, not on the reaction: the reaction continues above the studied interval, but the sampling method fails there, and the record stops where the method stops. A user of these figures who needs a constant beyond the interval must obtain it by another sampling route, because the present record offers no measured point against which an extrapolation could be checked. The record is also silent on the direction in which sampling failed first: evaporation during sampling is stated as the operative difficulty, and the passage does not separate the effect of the solvent loss on the sample from any effect on the reaction mixture itself. What the record supports is the pair of constants, the precision attached to the measurements, the derived standing of the upper value, and the stated reason for the absence of any higher point.
